summary: Specifies the frame format for sending IPv6 packets over an IPv4 domain, and how to form IPv6 link-local addresses, without explicit tunnels. It treats an IPv4 multicast network as a virtual link, and defines the link-layer address option used in neighbor discovery messages.

eli5.summary: Instead of building a private tunnel, this lets new-style internet messages ride across the old-style network by treating it like one big shared room.

questions: how does ipv6 over ipv4 multicast work
what is the default mtu for 6over4
how is a 6over4 link-local address formed
subtitle: Lets isolated IPv6 hosts use an IPv4 multicast network as a virtual Ethernet, with no configured tunnels.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 host on a link with no IPv6 router nearby is cut off from IPv6, and setting up explicit tunnels or IPv4-compatible addresses for it is a chore.
tldr.mechanism: IPv6 packets ride inside IPv4 packets with protocol type 41. The IPv4 multicast network acts as the IPv6 link, and the host's IPv4 address forms its interface identifier and link-local address.
tldr.outcome: Hosts become fully functional IPv6 hosts as soon as one IPv6 router using the same method is attached to the same IPv4 domain, a step in the move from IPv4 to IPv6.

today: RFC 2529 is a Proposed Standard published in March 1999. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the text presents it as one option among the transition mechanisms from IPv4 to IPv6.

sections.title: A Virtual Ethernet over IPv4
sections.content:
RFC 2529 specifies how to send IPv6 packets over an IPv4 domain: a fully interconnected set of IPv4 subnets, within the same local multicast scope, with at least two IPv6 nodes that follow the specification. The mechanism is known formally as "IPv6 over IPv4" or "6over4" and colloquially as "virtual Ethernet".

The goal is to let isolated IPv6 hosts, on a physical link with no directly connected IPv6 router, become fully functional by treating the IPv4 multicast domain as their virtual local link. If routing to other links is needed, at least one IPv6 router using the same method must be connected to the same IPv4 domain. The hosts need neither IPv4-compatible addresses nor configured tunnels.
sections.eli5: The old network pretends to be one big shared room for the new kind of messages. Kids in the room can talk to each other without any private tunnels.

sections.title: Frame Format and MTU
sections.content:
An IPv6 packet is carried in an IPv4 packet with an IPv4 protocol type of 41, the same value that RFC 1933 assigned for IPv6 packets tunneled inside IPv4. The IPv4 packet body holds the IPv6 header followed immediately by the payload. If IPv4 options are present, padding SHOULD be added so the IPv6 header starts on a 32-bit boundary from the end of the datalink header.

The default MTU for IPv6 packets on an IPv4 domain is 1480 octets. A Router Advertisement with an MTU option, or manual configuration of each node, can change it. If the MTU is too large for some IPv4 subnet, IPv4 fragmentation follows. The RFC calls this undesirable but not disastrous, yet the IPv4 "do not fragment" bit MUST NOT be set.

The Time to Live field SHOULD be set low so packets do not leak out of the IPv4 domain. It MUST be configurable, with a recommended default of 8.
sections.eli5: Each new-style message is put inside an old-style envelope marked with the number 41. The envelope is a little smaller than usual, and it is told to stop travelling after a few hops so it stays inside the room.

sections.title: Link-Local Addresses
sections.content:
The interface identifier of an IPv4 interface is its 32-bit IPv4 address, octets in the same order as in an IPv4 header, padded on the left with zeros to 64 bits. The Universal/Local bit is zero, so the identifier is not globally unique. If the host has more than one IPv4 address on that interface, an administrative choice picks one.

The IPv6 link-local address is formed by appending this identifier to the prefix FE80::/64. A prefix used for stateless autoconfiguration of an IPv4 interface MUST be 64 bits long, except for the special case in the transition discussion.
sections.eli5: Your new-style address is made by taking your old-style address and putting a standard prefix and some zeros in front of it. It is like adding an area code to a phone number you already have.

sections.title: Mapping Unicast Addresses
sections.content:
Finding the IPv4 address for an IPv6 neighbor follows the procedure in RFC 2461. The Source/Target Link-layer Address option, used in Router Solicitation, Router Advertisement, Neighbor Solicitation, Neighbor Advertisement and Redirect messages, takes a specific form when the link layer is IPv4.

Its Type is 1 for a Source Link-layer address and 2 for a Target Link-layer address. Its Length is 1, because the unit is 8 octets. After two bytes that must be zero comes the 32-bit IPv4 address in network byte order. That is the address the interface currently responds to, which may differ from the interface identifier used for autoconfiguration.
sections.eli5: When a computer asks who owns a new-style address, the answer is a tiny card carrying the owner's old-style address. That tells everyone where to actually send the envelope.

sections.title: Mapping Multicast Addresses
sections.content:
IPv4 multicast MUST be available. An IPv6 packet sent to a multicast address is transmitted to an IPv4 multicast address of Organization-Local Scope. These addresses SHOULD come from the block 239.192.0.0/16, or, if those are not all available, from the expansion blocks defined in RFC 2365, of which only a /16 is used.

The IPv4 address has the form 239.OLS.DST14.DST15. DST14 and DST15 are the last two bytes of the IPv6 multicast address, and OLS comes from the configured Organization-Local Scope block and SHOULD be 192. No new IANA registration procedures are required.

Appendix A lists the groups needed for Neighbor Discovery: all-nodes is 239.OLS.0.1 and all-routers is 239.OLS.0.2. A solicited-node address for an IPv4 address W.X.Y.Z maps to 239.OLS.Y.Z.
sections.eli5: Group messages go to a shared mailing address in the old network. The last two numbers of the new-style group address are copied into the old-style one, so everybody interested listens at the same spot.

sections.title: Scaling and Transition
sections.content:
The RFC expects multicast here to scale much like native IPv6 on most media, apart from a slightly smaller MTU that slightly reduces bulk throughput. On an ATM network, where IPv4 multicast relies on relatively complex mechanisms, it expects IPv6 over IPv4 over ATM to perform less well than native IPv6 over ATM.

The mechanism is meant as one option for the move from IPv4 to IPv6. A site can configure one IPv6 router with 6over4 on an interface facing its IPv4 domain, and another IPv6 format on an interface facing the IPv6 Internet. Enabled hosts can then talk to the router and the IPv6 Internet with no manual tunnel and no IPv4-compatible address.

Routers may need to advertise two prefixes, one for the native LAN and one for 6over4, and the 6over4 prefix MUST be unique within its scope. If a router serves both on one physical interface, both use FE80::/64 during autoconfiguration, so the prefix length of those link-local addresses MUST then be 128 to tell them apart. Later, hosts that become adjacent to IPv6 routers can switch to native IPv6.
sections.eli5: This is a bridge to use while everyone slowly moves to the new system. Once a native route is built next to you, you can step off the bridge.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementors must consider attacks against IPv4 as well as IPv6. The RFC advises avoiding IP security at both levels for efficiency: if IPv6 is encrypted, encrypting IPv4 is redundant except where traffic analysis is a threat. IPv4 security will not protect IPv6 traffic once it leaves the domain, so IPv6 security is required even if IPv4 security is available.

Spurious 6over4 packets could be injected from outside. Boundary routers MUST discard IPv4 multicast packets with organization-local scope source or destination addresses arriving on interfaces outside that scope. They MUST also discard incoming protocol type 41 packets from unknown sources. Unless IPSEC authentication is available, the RECOMMENDED technique is to accept type 41 packets only from a trusted range or ranges of source addresses.
sections.eli5: The guards at the doors of the room must turn away strangers trying to slip fake messages in. Only envelopes from known senders may enter.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: 1 for Source Link-layer address, 2 for Target.

fields.name: IPv4 Address
fields.desc: The 32-bit IPv4 address in network byte order.
